explanations.explanation: Yes, sackcloth is the first one. The LORD tells Isaiah, "Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist…" (Isaiah 20:2). Sackcloth was the rough cloth Isaiah wore around his waist. I wear an apron around mine, and I'd feel pretty exposed without it.

Yes, sandals are the second one. The LORD says to remove "…the sandals from your feet." (Isaiah 20:2). So Isaiah goes without anything on his feet. Even on a cookie planet, I'd hate to step on a stray crumb with bare feet.

Close, but a cloak isn't in the verse. The LORD names the sackcloth from Isaiah's waist and the sandals from his feet (Isaiah 20:2). The cloak is a fair guess, since it's clothing too. But the text only names those two things.

A belt is a fair guess for something at the waist, but it's not in the verse. The LORD says to remove the sackcloth from Isaiah's waist (Isaiah 20:2). It's the sackcloth that comes off. The feet are covered by the other answer, the sandals.

No anklets here. The LORD's command is plain: take the sackcloth off the waist and the sandals off the feet (Isaiah 20:2). Anklets sound fancy, but nothing in the verse says Isaiah wore any. I'd have to see that jingle to believe it.

This one's False. The LORD gives the command, "And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot." (Isaiah 20:2). The text shows no pushback and no request for another sign. If I had been handed that command, I think I'd have asked about ten questions first.

Right, it's False. After the LORD's command, the text says, "And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot." (Isaiah 20:2). No argument and no asking for a different sign. Isaiah just does it. Friend, that is a hard thing to do, and he did it.

Yes! The LORD says Isaiah went naked and barefoot "…as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush," (Isaiah 20:3). Cush is the land south of Egypt. Three years of walking around like that was a message for them, not just a strange habit.

Moab and Edom are other nations in the Bible, but they aren't named here. The LORD says the sign is "…against Egypt and Cush," (Isaiah 20:3). Those two are the ones in this passage. I'd put Moab and Edom back on the shelf for now.

Babylon and Persia are big names, but they aren't in these verses. The LORD says Isaiah's three years are "…a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush," (Isaiah 20:3). The king doing the leading away here is the king of Assyria (Isaiah 20:4). It's easy to mix up the big empires, but this passage names Egypt and Cush.

explanations.answer: They'll be led away naked and barefoot
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says the king of Assyria "…will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot…" (Isaiah 20:4). What Isaiah has been doing is what the captives will look like. The sign and the real thing match.

explanations.answer: They'll be put to work building cities
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says the king of Assyria will lead the captives away "…naked and barefoot…" (Isaiah 20:4). Nothing about building cities appears in these verses. I'll admit, a work crew in hard hats would've made for a different story.

explanations.answer: They'll be locked away in prisons
explanations.explanation: Prisons aren't mentioned here. The LORD says the captives will be led away "…naked and barefoot…" (Isaiah 20:4). That's the picture the text gives. Sticking to what it says keeps us on solid ground.
Yes, True. The LORD says the king of Assyria will lead away the captives and exiles, "…young and old alike…" (Isaiah 20:4). Nobody gets skipped. Young and old are both in the line.

This one's True. The LORD says the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush will be led away, "…young and old alike…" (Isaiah 20:4). Both ages are named right there in the verse. It's easy to miss in a verse that's got a lot going on.
Yes, shame. The LORD says the king of Assyria will lead them away "…to Egypt’s shame." (Isaiah 20:4). It was a public, humbling sight. The thing Egypt was proud of ends up being what embarrasses it.

Honor is the opposite of what the verse says. The LORD says the captives will be led away "…to Egypt’s shame." (Isaiah 20:4). There's no parade or medal for Egypt in this passage. Not a single cookie of honor to go around.
No relief in this verse. The LORD says the captives are led away "…to Egypt’s shame." (Isaiah 20:4). Shame is the word the text uses. Relief would be a nice ending, but that's not what's written.

explanations.answer: Those who hoped in Egypt and Cush
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, "Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed." (Isaiah 20:5). They had put their hope in those two lands. When Egypt and Cush are shamed, the people counting on them are let down too.

explanations.answer: Those who fought against Egypt and Cush
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't talk about people who fought against them. It says those who "…made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast…" will be dismayed and ashamed (Isaiah 20:5). So it's the ones who counted on Egypt and Cush. That's a different group from their opponents.

explanations.answer: Those who were enslaved by Egypt and Cush
explanations.explanation: Slaves aren't mentioned in this passage. The LORD says it's those who "…made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast…" who will be dismayed and ashamed (Isaiah 20:5). Those people were leaning on Egypt and Cush for hope. That's the group the verse is after.

Yes. The coastland dwellers say, "…How then can we escape?" (Isaiah 20:6). They had fled to Egypt and Cush for help against the king of Assyria. Now their source of hope is the one being led away. I think they're feeling pretty stuck.

explanations.answer: Who will be our king now
explanations.explanation: A king isn't what they ask about. The coastland dwellers say, "…How then can we escape?" (Isaiah 20:6). Their worry is about getting away from the king of Assyria. They had gone to Egypt and Cush for that very thing.

explanations.answer: Where can we hide our gold now
explanations.explanation: Gold isn't in this passage at all. The coastland dwellers ask, "…How then can we escape?" (Isaiah 20:6). They're thinking about escaping the king of Assyria, not their treasure. Hiding gold would be a different story.
